course.title: AP World History: Modern
course.description: Understand the people, ideas, and connections that shaped the world from c. 1200 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Explore how states rose, belief systems spread, trade networks connected regions, and revolutions reshaped societies from c. 1200 to the present.

unit.title: Global Conflict
unit.description: Study how empires collapsed, why two world wars were fought and how they were conducted, how the Depression reshaped economies, and how mass atrocities happened.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an example of total war during World War I?
choices: Civilians remaining unaffected by the war
Governments leaving industry entirely to private owners
Governments rationing food and directing industry

questions.explanation: Rationing and state direction of industry mobilized whole societies.

questions.distinguisher: Governments took control of industry rather than leaving it alone.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 7.3 key concept: World War I was the first total war, in which governments used propaganda and directed economies to mobilize entire populations
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing total war in 1914–1918
stimulusBlocks.text:
World War I was a total war. Governments took control of industries, rationed food, and drafted millions of men. With men at the front, women took jobs in factories, offices, and transportation. Propaganda posters and newspapers portrayed the enemy as monstrous and urged civilians to buy war bonds.

New weapons made the fighting deadly. Machine guns and artillery forced armies into trenches on the Western Front, and attacks across open ground killed hundreds of thousands for small gains. Poison gas, first used on a large scale in 1915, and tanks, introduced in 1916, did not break the stalemate.

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, poison gas and tanks
choices: ended the war in 1915
were used only at sea
broke the stalemate in 1916
did not break the stalemate
questions.explanation: The passage says they did not break the stalemate.
choiceExplanations: The passage says they did not break the stalemate.
questions.distinguisher: The passage says they did not break it.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, about how many people from India served Britain in the war?
choices: About 1.3 million
About 140,000

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 7.3 key concept: imperial powers recruited soldiers and laborers from their colonies to fight World War I
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing colonial participation in World War I
stimulusBlocks.text:
About 1.3 million soldiers and laborers from India served Britain in the war, in France, the Middle East, and East Africa. France recruited soldiers from West Africa, North Africa, and Indochina. China, which was neutral at first, sent about 140,000 laborers to work behind the lines in France.

Many colonial soldiers expected their service to be rewarded with greater rights. When the peace brought little change, disappointment fueled demands for self-government.

questions.prompt: The passage suggests that colonial service in the war led to
choices: satisfaction with colonial rule
the end of the British Empire in 1919
a ban on colonial soldiers
demands for self-government
questions.distinguisher: Disappointment, not satisfaction, followed the peace.

questions.prompt: Which factors does the passage cite as making infantry attacks costly?
choices: Tanks, aircraft, and poison gas
Shortages of food and ammunition
Machine guns, barbed wire, and artillery
Lack of training among soldiers
questions.explanation: The passage says these defensive weapons made attacks extremely costly.
choiceExplanations: The passage lists these as new weapons that did not break the stalemate.
The passage does not cite shortages as the reason.
The passage says these defensive weapons made attacks extremely costly.
The passage does not discuss training.
questions.distinguisher: Tanks and gas were new weapons, but the passage presents them as attempts to end the stalemate.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 7.3 key concept: trench warfare and new weapons made World War I a war of attrition
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing fighting on the Western Front, 1914–1918
stimulusBlocks.text:
On the Western Front after 1914, armies dug trenches that stretched from the English Channel to Switzerland. Machine guns, barbed wire, and artillery made infantry attacks extremely costly. At Verdun in 1916, French and German forces fought for ten months and suffered about 700,000 casualties combined. At the Somme later that year, British forces suffered nearly 60,000 casualties on the first day of the battle.

Both sides tried new weapons, including poison gas, tanks, and aircraft, but the front moved only a few miles. The stalemate ended in 1918, when Germany's spring offensives failed, American troops arrived in large numbers, and Allied armies advanced.

questions.prompt: The situation on the Western Front most directly resulted in
choices: a quick German victory over France in 1914
heavy casualties and a search for new weapons
a decline in the use of artillery in war
widespread peace negotiations in 1915 and 1916
questions.explanation: Attacks failed against strong defenses, so both sides tried gas, tanks, and aircraft.
choiceExplanations: The passage describes a stalemate lasting until 1918.
Attacks failed against strong defenses, so both sides tried gas, tanks, and aircraft.
The passage describes major battles in 1916 and no early peace.
questions.distinguisher: Germany hoped for a quick victory in 1914, but trench warfare ended that hope.

questions.prompt: The arrival of American troops in 1918 mattered because
choices: it gave the Allies fresh troops as Germany tired
it forced the Allies to give up the trenches they held
it ended Britain's naval blockade of Germany

questions.explanation: American troops joined the Allies as Germany's spring offensives failed.
